metadata.title: Form and Function in Ancient Writing Systems: A Spectral Companion to Computational Paleography
metadata.description: Recent advances in computational paleography (Zemene et al., 2026) applied neural networks to over 28,000 glyph images, identifying significant visual and structural alignments between ancient Ethiopic (Ge'ez) and historical scripts of the Caucasus (most notably Classical Armenian). That work established an objective metric for visual form: stroke curves, angles, and 2D geometric topology. This report delivers the complementary analysis of linguistic function: evaluating writing systems as deterministic discrete dynamical systems . Under the Engineering of Alphabets (EOA) framework, letter names are treated as deterministic recursive sequence engines. Using exact arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic (BigInt Berlekamp–Massey), Frobenius normal form decomposition, and spectral graph theory, we extract the minimal recurrences, characteristic polynomials, and dominant Perron eigenvalues (λ) that govern each script. Across the five target writing systems (totaling 178 individual letters: Ge'ez, Caucasian Albanian, Georgian, Classical Armenian, and Old South Arabian), we establish five distinct structural profiles: The Golden Ratio Core (Ge’ez, φ² ≈ 2.618): Features a 12-letter recurrent core whose sequences satisfy an exact second-order Fibonacci-bisection recurrence, coupled to a 14-letter transient periphery. The Low-Collapse Network (Caucasian Albanian, λ ≈ 2.956): 46 of 49 sequence groups are single letters, yet all 52 letters lock into an identical asymptotic growth constant. The High-Collapse Core (Georgian, λ ≈ 2.521): 33 letters collapse into 11 sequence groups (including an 11-letter consonant block and a 5-letter vowel block) sharing a coupled growth rate. The Decomposed Regime (Armenian): Fragments into 25 distinct internal sequence groups displaying bimodal growth (polynomial and base-2 exponential), demonstrating a divergence between visual form and recurrence dynamics. metadata.title: The Budargham EOA Sequence Census
metadata.description: This dataset presents the 346 uncatalogued integer sequences generated by the Engineering of Alphabets (EOA) operator applied to 36 historical writing systems. Derived from the incidence matrices of 36 scripts totaling 1,056 individual letters, these sequences represent the raw mathematical output of alphabet structures that do not currently appear in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS). To establish priority and facilitate peer review, this release documents the first 15 terms of each sequence, alongside its limiting growth rate, characteristic polynomial, and the script(s) that generate it. The sequences are organized into the "Budargham EOA Sequence Family" and categorized by their dominant algebraic constants (e.g. φ²≈2.618 , 1+√2≈2.414, 2+√2≈3.414). Sequences that do not fall into these core algebraic families are grouped as "uncatalogued_other" and sorted by their exact limiting growth rates, demonstrating the high-order structural complexity of the census. Data Access and Restrictions: The 36 open incidence matrices used to generate these counts are available at their permanent DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23440579. The full 500-term sequences and the underlying generating operator algorithm are currently under a separate agreement and are not included in this release. By providing these prefixes alongside the open matrices, this release enables researchers to reproduce the initial terms and invites the community to conduct adjacency audits and further structural analysis of the sequences.

metadata.title: A Grammar of  Kusaal
metadata.description: A reference grammar of the Agolle dialect of Kusaal, a Gur language of Northern Ghana.

metadata.title: A Grammar of  Kusaal
metadata.description: A reference grammar of the Agolle dialect of Kusaal, a Gur language of Northern Ghana. A more recent version may be at www.academia.edu/30678520

metadata.title: Variation, acquisition and change
metadata.description: Humans are seemingly unique in the animal kingdom in that we have language; systems enabling communication about any topic, be it past, present or future. In fact, humans are not limited to one language but can acquire several under the right conditions. Although undoubtedly a cultural object, language is also a fundamental part of the mind/brain of a human being, the constitution of which we refer to as a mental grammar. Changes in states of linguistic knowledge, whether in development (acquisition), over the lifespan or across generations (change) examined across diverse populations and language combinations (variation), provide crucial insights about the organization of mental grammars. This volume, entitled Variation, Acquisition and Change, brings together research on language acquisition in different populations, language change in various languages, and linguistic variation from an empirical and a theoretical perspective. The chapters illuminate these issues from a range of different methodological, empirical, and theoretical perspectives. Importantly, many chapters also combine two or three of the themes, illustrating that they are linked and that such combinations increase our understanding of a given linguistic phenomenon.

metadata.title: Approaches to L3 phonological acquisition research: challenges, considerations, best practices
metadata.description: This contribution aims at a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art approaches to research on L3 phonological acquisition. The analysis involves theoretical and methodological considerations as well as practical solutions to problems pertaining to the production, perception and processing of speech in third and additional languages. A range of research paradigms, elicitation tasks, and instruments are critically evaluated and various approaches to auditory and acoustic analyses are discussed. The overview is illustrated with examples from current research into L3 phonetics and phonology including the findings from the most recent Polish-Norwegian project.

metadata.title: Multilingualism and syntactic change in English 1400--1700
metadata.description: This chapter will bring together recent work on the loss of Verb Second (V2) in English with insights from the literature on the rise of do-support and on the auxiliation of modal auxiliaries. It adds to the discussion of the interrelatedness between these changes, which form a key part of the reorganization of the English verbal system from late Middle English (ME) to the end of early Modern English (EME) and beyond. This complex of changes will also be considered from the perspective of increasing language and dialect contact that I will discuss from the point of view of multilingualism.

metadata.title: The nanosyntax of Norwegian \textit som
metadata.description: The Norwegian item som is used in a wide range of constructions, ranging from equative and essive constructions to relative clauses and embedded wh-questions, and in some varieties it is even used in comparatives and matrix subject wh-questions. This chapter discusses the various uses in a comparative perspective mainly against other Germanic varieties, arriving at an understanding of the wide lexicalization range as reflexes of historical grammaticalization that involves step-by-step cumulative expansion from smaller syntactic structures to bigger ones. Under a nanosyntactic approach this can in turn be understood as gradual growth regarding the specification of what sub-trees som may lexicalize.

metadata.title: Categorization of novel nouns with ambiguous gender cues: Experimental evidence from Russian
metadata.description: This chapter reports on an experimental study investigating the role of probabilistic rules in gender assignment to ambiguously cued novel nouns by adult monolingual speakers of Russian. Unlike previous works on the topic, the study is large in scale (267 participants jointly providing around 35000 gender judgments) and comprehensive in scope (1648 ambiguous monosyllabic stimuli including all possible phonotactically licit combinations of cue-bearing phonological units--codas, nuclei and onsets). The main results indicate that speakers can reliably access probabilistic rules to classify novel nouns into gender classes based on their phonological properties, and the information relevant for gender assignment is generalized at the level of segment classes captured by binary phonological features [± sonorant] (codas), [±continuant] (onsets), as well as [±high] and [±low] (nuclei).

metadata.title: A spanning approach to the categories of the English verb and their linearization
metadata.description: In English, auxiliaries linearize in the T position, preceding medial adverbs, while lexical verbs linearize in the verb phrase, following medial adverbs. In a span-based approach to word order, linearization of words in the extended projection is determined by the position of a spell-out label @. The English pattern suggests that the distribution of @ is not a fixed property of a head like T, but is partly dependent on the category of the complement of that head. I propose to encode this observation in a functional lexicon which is not simply an unstructured set of formatives, but is organized into a finite state automaton, where properties of the functional lexicon are distributed over the states and transitions. The finite state automaton defines an extended projection. States encode properties which are fixed for a category, where category is defined in terms of distribution. Transitions carry information that can vary with the lower category in the extended projection, including information affecting linearization.

metadata.title: The effectiveness of cues in gender processing by Russian-speaking children
metadata.description: Eye movements of 27 Russian-speaking 5-to-6-year-old children who viewed 4-picture animated displays in a Visual World study were recorded. Participants listened to “In the sky flew.f [a] silver.f bird.f” and clicked on the Target ‘bird.f’. In the 2x2 design, the gender of the Target (M/F) was crossed with referential ambiguity in the visual display, i.e., two referents of the same gender (AMB) vs. only one (UNAMB). The accuracy in clicking on the Target was at ceiling: 97%. The cluster-based permutation analysis of eye movements (1,000 permutations) that predicted the empirical logit of proportion of fixations to the Target, identified only one late significant cluster where the looks to the Target were higher in UNAMB than AMB conditions. Thus, children used gender agreement cues only in the facilitatory manner, F cues were no more perceptually salient than M cues in the early adjective region, and did not benefit from cue coalition, i.e., the doubling of cues. These results can be best explained by complexity of the design combined with the less efficient gender agreement cues in Russian.

metadata.title: Exploring the Micro-Cue Model: Contextual and referential effects on sentence comprehension in Russian-German bilingual children
metadata.description: Preschoolers often exhibit difficulties comprehending non-canonical OVS sentences, possibly due to factors related to processing, information structure and/or case marking. We examined how topic-first contexts, pronominal topics and language proficiency influence offline OVS comprehension in the dual languages of Russian-German bilingual. The topic-first context did not influence OVS accuracy in neither language. When the object was realized as a pronoun in OVS sentences, comprehension accuracy improved in Russian but not in German. We discuss the results by adapting the Micro-cue model (Westergaard 2009, 2014) to comprehension: a) children start from more specific structures that are later gen- eralized, b) children are sensitive to information structure from early on, and c) comprehension is influenced by issues of economy.

metadata.title: Maintaining word order flexibility in contact with a V2 grammar: Evidence from semi-spontaneous narratives of Norwegian-Russian bilingual children
metadata.description: This study investigates word order patterns in semi-spontaneous spoken narratives produced by Russian-speaking children living in Norway (n=27, mean age=6;7). The analysis of the distribution of subject-initial vs. non-subject-initial declarative main clauses, as well as the verb positioning in relation to overtly expressed subjects and objects, shows that Norwegian-Russian children operate two distinct grammars: the Russian word order grammar, which closely resembles that of monolinguals, and differs from their Norwegian word order grammar. In other words, there is no indication of a quantitative or qualitative reduction in word order flexibility in heritage Russian, nor is there strong evidence that the Norwegian verb second order is affected by cross-linguistic influence from Russian.

metadata.title: Micro-cues are spans
metadata.description: In this chapter, we explore the notion that micro-cues (Westergaard 2009a,b, 2014, 2021) can aid in conceptualizing the observed conservative nature of gains and changes in (multilingual) language acquisition, historical syntactic change, and dialect variation. In a related sense, segments of syntactic structures commonly known as spans (Blix 2021a,b; Svenonius 2016, 2020) share a number of similarities with micro-cues; e.g., sub-segments of larger hierarchical structures, both consisting of contiguous heads and features, etc. In this chapter, we introduce and support the claim that micro-cues are inherently spans. We support this thesis by demonstrating how a spanning-based approach is capable of accounting for the acquisition and historical development of elements of syntax.

metadata.title: Plural generic statements in Norwegian as L3
metadata.description: This study investigates the effect of previously acquired languages on the acquisition of article use in generic and specific NPs in Norwegian as a third language (L3); in particular, how multilinguals acquire the form-to-meaning mapping (FMM) between the universal meaning of genericity and its expressions by plural noun phrases. We tested three learner groups: English native speakers residing in Norway and two groups of Polish speakers with English as an L2, one group residing in Norway, and the other group enrolled in Norwegian classes at university in Poland. We hypothesized that all learners would be highly accurate with the bare plural, as it is a shared FMM. In contrast, the Polish speakers were expected to be less accurate in accepting the definite plural form, given that Polish lacks definite marking with articles. We tested our hypotheses using a truth value judgment task providing generic and non-generic contexts, with test sentence subjects expressed as either bare or definite plurals. Our findings indicate that all learner groups had acquired the Norwegian FMMs, although the English group demonstrated higher accuracy compared to the Polish groups. Unexpectedly, the Polish speakers showed higher accuracy with the definite than with the bare form, and the foreign language learners were more accurate compared to the immersed learners. We argue that this is a consequence of the learner setting, i.e., the foreign language learners receiving more explicit instruction on article use. Additionally, we argue that dialectal variation in the expression of the definite plural form may have influenced the responses of the immersed learners.

metadata.title: Is a center a unit or a group of individuals? Agreement of Norwegian predicate adjectives
metadata.description: In this article, we explore the polysemous Norwegian word senter ‘center’ and similar collective nouns, focusing on their agreement properties. Based on corpus data, we show that the relevant collective nouns can combine with predicate adjectives in both the singular and the plural. We relate the distribution to the “agency hypothesis” (Nesset et al. 2022), whereby plural agreement is favored when predicate adjectives imply carrying out an action, and the “individuation hypothesis” (Nesset & Janda 2023), according to which plural agreement is favored when a collective noun is conceptualized as a group of individuals. Our findings support Westergaard’s (2014) idea about “micro-cues”, whereby children are sensitive to fine syntactic distinctions from early on.

metadata.title: Subordination in Swedish narratives of monolingual and bilingual children
metadata.description: This paper investigates clausal subordination in oral narratives elicited from 72 monolingual Swedish and 102 bilingual Turkish/Swedish children age 4$-$7, keeping task and context constant. The cross-sectional analysis shows a clear increase in the frequency and variety of subordinate clauses with age for both groups, which suggests that children's expressive Swedish language competence in the domain of subordination develops strongly beyond age 4;0, unlike earlier claims in the literature. Subordinators are very rarely omitted. The monolinguals produce higher proportions of subordinate clauses than their bilingual age-peers, and the difference between the groups is particularly evident for relative clauses. Implications for language assessment in clinical practice are discussed. The study adds knowledge in a domain where empirical work has so far concentrated on case studies of monolingual Swedish children age 2--3.

metadata.title: Processing of locative prepositional phrases by young children: An eye-tracking study
metadata.description: In this study, we use Visual World eye-tracking to investigate the processing of locative PPs by Russian-speaking 2- and 3-year-old children (n=63). Experimental trials involved pictures representing contrasting locative configurations: "in" vs "under" and "on" vs "behind". The relevant linguistic cues involved locative prepositions and case marking on the Ground NP: "in" and "on" assign locative case, while "under" and "behind" assign instrumental case. In the control condition, pictures differed in the choice of objects involved (figure or ground). The analysis revealed a significant positive effect of age group in the experimental conditions which went beyond the differences observed in the control conditions. This suggests that the 3-year-olds' better performance on locative PP comprehension cannot be fully explained by attention to the task or differences in the processing of lexical nouns. These results align with previously reported production patterns, with 2- but not 3-year-olds omitting a substantial portion of prepositions from their early utterances and support the Underspecified P account of preposition omission at the telegraphic speech stage (Mitrofanova2017)

metadata.title: Cross-linguistic influence and the role of micro-cues in gender assignment: Ukrainian refugee children acquiring Polish
metadata.description: Over 6 million Ukrainians were forced to leave their homes and sought refuge in Europe as the result of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with over 2 million of them being children. These children faced the need to rapidly learn the languages of their new host countries and adapt to schooling in the new language. We present an elicited production study aimed at investigating the acquisition of grammatical gender in the new language, Polish, with a special focus on morpho-phonological gender cues. Our experimental group are Ukrainian children aged 6--12 years (n = 64), who have been living in Poland for 4--77 months and acquiring Polish in an immersive context. We compare them to monolingual speakers of the same age (n = 30). Our findings indicate that bilingual children tended to use feminine agreement with palatalized consonants, which serve as ambiguous gender cues, more often than their monolingual peers, particularly for the '-ć' cue. This tendency increased with age, suggesting a stronger cross-linguistic influence from the L1 in older children.

metadata.title: Unshifted subjects or shifting particles? On the acquisition of particle and subject placement
metadata.description: Young speakers in certain areas of Norway display a word order deviation regarding placement of the subject with respect to verb particles: Both children and teenagers occasionally place verb particles in front of subjects in non-subject-initial clauses, in contrast to the adult pattern. In this article we investigate whether this word order deviation is a result of a particle shifting across the subject, or a subject surfacing in situ, i.e., inside the verb phrase. Based on spontaneous and elicited examples of particle placement from children and teenagers, we can observe a development in which the particle placement becomes increasingly target-like. Still, the pattern observed goes against trends of economy and conservativity observed in other studies of word-order development: The children appear to start with a relatively free word order, which slowly becomes more restricted. As we will argue, the development is difficult to describe in terms of preference either for or against syntactic movement.

metadata.title: Bilectalism, dominance, and micro-cues: Vowel insertion and deletion in Brazilian and European Portuguese bilectals
metadata.description: European Portuguese speaking Brazilians who acquired European Portuguese late in life (late bilectals) were rated as more Brazilian-sounding than speakers who acquired EP early in life (early bilectals). Both groups show traces of the other variety in each speaking mode (European and Brazilian Portuguese, respectively), which distinguishes them from monolectals. We propose that this is best accounted for in a model of indexed violable constraints, where a basic ranking and indexed constraints are activated for the different varieties if rankings diverge. Cross-linguistic influence (CLI) emerges from two sources. First, micro-cues are not detected and the corresponding differences in Elementary Ranking Conditions are not implemented as reranking/indexation. Moreover, constraint indexes may occasionally be switched on/off for the wrong variety or lost entirely, resulting in a permanent ranking deviance from the respective monolectal ranking.

metadata.title: Cross-linguistic influence in L3 Norwegian: An empirical study of Ukrainian-English speakers in Norway
metadata.description: In this empirical study, we build on previous L3 work by examining the L3 acquisition of Norwegian among L1 Ukrainian-L2 English multilinguals using an adapted method presented in van Osch et al. (2023). Specifically, we conduct a gap filling task on adverb placement based on similarities and differences in the languages, which allows us to identify whether cross-linguistic influence (CLI), if present, comes from the L1, the L2 or both previously acquired languages. Based on related results and analyses (Kolb et al. 2022, 2023, van Osch et al. 2023), we anticipate CLI from both previously acquired languages. Our findings show that L3 learners have acquired surface-level Norwegian word order in main clauses and overgeneralize the same pattern to subordinate clauses. We did not find evidence for surface-level CLI from L1 Ukrainian or L2 English. While our results do not support direct CLI from either Ukrainian or English, analyzing them through the lens of the Linguistic Proximity Model (LPM, Mykhaylyk et al. 2015; Westergaard et al. 2017; Westergaard et al. 2019), requires us to consider more abstract patterns of CLI based on individual structural properties. This perspective leads us to new questions to pursue in future studies.

metadata.title: Using production data to study pragmatic development
metadata.description: While production data, in particular those including spontaneous speech, have been considered a useful source of evidence in studies of the development of grammar, their adequacy for studies of pragmatic development has been questioned. Production data for pragmatic phenomena are often hard to interpret and typically thought to underestimate children's performance compared to comprehension data. In this paper we survey a set of studies using production data, both spontaneous and elicited, to investigate children's language development, including pragmatic aspects. We argue that they provide a valuable source of evidence, especially for studies of early pragmatic development and phenomena where controlled comprehension experiments may not be feasible to run with a given age group, for instance when studying subtle intonational differences or non-literal uses of language. Finally, we discuss to what extent production data can be seen as providing a window into children's developing pragmatic competence.

metadata.title: Naming what has not been done
metadata.description: Fábregas & González Rodríguez (2020) analyse inhibited events as instances where negation is merged low, over Init(iation)P, with the effect that causation is reinterpreted as inhibition (not-causation) of an event. This predicts that there should be instances of lexical verbs whose initiation layer actually means exerting force to inhibit an event that otherwise was expected to happen. This chapter argues that the prediction is borne out and provides examples from Spanish, showing that their behaviour is the one predicted by the original analysis.

metadata.title: Eliciting grammatical gender: Some methodological reflections
metadata.description: A frequently used behavioral task to study grammatical gender involves a picture-based elicitation task. For Norwegian, Rodina & Westergaard (2015) adopted a paradigm originally developed by Blom et al. (2008) for grammatical gender. Since then, this paradigm has been used by many scholars (Busterud et al. 2019, Rodina & Westergaard 2021, van Baal et al. 2023) to elicit indefinite and definite determiners and prenominal and postnominal possessives. As part of the research project Grammatical Gender in Norwegian Dialects: Variation, Acquisition & Change (GenVAC), we developed this methodology further so that we also could elicit plurals and anaphoric pronouns. Elicitation data have been crucial in demonstrating that the Norwegian grammatical gender system is in the process of being reduced from three grammatical genders (masculine, feminine, and neuter) to two (common and neuter). In this chapter, we discuss methodological challenges that emerge when trying to capture a changing grammatical gender system using elicitation tasks. We will discuss the methodological choices made in the GenVAC project, including both positive and negative consequences. In particular, we see that participants produce more feminine markers as the experiment session progresses, and we discuss some factors that may explain this result, involving the availability of more than one gender system in the input, lexical effects, the role of the interviewer, and task effects more generally.

metadata.title: Movement, morphology and Middle English multilingualism: A perfect storm of grammatical events
metadata.description: The great restructuring of English grammar emerged via many separate morphosyntactic developments all related to the morphosyntactic finiteness feature, constituting a linguistic "perfect storm" occurring in a period of intense language contact. The finiteness distinction is notoriously hard to acquire for contemporary second language learners of Germanic languages; favoring the prototypical grammatical template where modals are finite. They prefer modals and (dummy) auxiliaries as exponents of finiteness and show a prolonged reluctance to move main verbs. As morphological cues of finiteness eroded in English, infinitives and participial forms of main verbs were lost (first with regular verbs), and many main verbs no longer encoded finiteness. This banned them from the V2 position, where finiteness is an absolute requirement. Do -support emerged to provide finiteness analytically, first to regular verbs. Irregular verbs maintained the finiteness distinction and kept their access to the V2 position for longer.

metadata.title: Dynamics of case in monolingual and bilingual first language acquisition of Russian
metadata.description: The acquisition of case in Russian, with its apparent variability in paths and timing, poses challenges for linguistic theories as the empirical evidence found in spontaneously elicited data is rather complex. This study investigates case acquisition by simultaneous bilinguals and compares it to monolingual acquisition using spontaneous longitudinal data from two bilingual and three monolingual participants. We track the phases in case marking acquisition and establish the developmental path of case in Russian. The findings show comparable timing and path of case acquisition across both groups, though bilingual children show dynamics in accusative case marking of a type resembling a U-shaped development with certain forms. Both bilingual and monolingual children also display overgeneralizations in the case inflections. These results suggest that while bilingual children may experience temporary setbacks, their overall developmental trajectory remains comparable to that of monolingual peers, provided they receive consistent input in Russian.

metadata.title: Directionality of cross-linguistic influence: Better insights from more comparisons
metadata.description: This review focuses on syntactic and morphosyntactic processing in bilinguals when they are compared to each other (bilingual-bilingual comparison) or when the two languages of bilinguals are compared (between-language comparison). The first comparison type is especially helpful in pinpointing whether there is cross-linguistic influence, as opposed to a single comparison between, for example, a mono- and bilingual child group. We show that, thus far, there is ample evidence for cross-linguistic influence (CLI) from an L1 to an L2, but it is less clear whether it may go in the opposite direction, not the least due to a lack of proper comparison groups. We thus examine bidirectional CLI in late bilingual adults (from the L2 to the L1), with a focus on regressive CLI (rCLI). We then explore bidirectional CLI in early bilingual children. Finally, we discuss how research could go forward in this burgeoning area.

metadata.title: A corpus study of verb placement in L3 French and L3 German: Insights from learner language
metadata.description: This exploratory study investigates verb placement in L3 French and German, respectively, in the written production of L1 Norwegian L2 English speakers in upper secondary schools. Verb placement in L3 in similar populations has been widely investigated using various experimental methods, generally concluding that L2 English plays a strong role in the cross-linguistic influence (CLI) observed in the L3. However, there is no consensus about whether this role is due to its L2 status or other reasons, nor about the impact that different methodologies may have on the findings. The present study seeks to complement existing knowledge focusing on the understudied area of written production. Overall findings suggest that the relevant structures are part of the learners' linguistic repertoire, and that patterns of CLI are similar to those found using other methodologies, indicating that these findings accurately reflect the underlying linguistic system. However, there is indication that CLI from either prior language is not the only explanation for learners' behavior in written production. Our data supports an analysis where general mechanisms such as principles of economy play a role in the acquisition of verb movement in L3.

metadata.title: Mian verbs trouble linguists not learners
metadata.description: Mian, a Papuan language of Papua New Guinea, shows an unusual system of verb agreement. All finite verbs obligatorily mark subject agreement, yet only a minority of transitive verbs show object agreement. This creates a striking split within the verbal lexicon. We investigate the morphological and syntactic implications of this restricted system, distinguishing it from more familiar types of inflectional irregularity (such as irregular past tense forms in English). While the absence of object agreement in Mian might appear to challenge learnability, we show that learners have robust cues: pervasive subject agreement, the higher token frequency of agreeing verbs relative to their type frequency, and the fact that a single verb form typically suffices to identify whether it shows object agreement. Comparative data from languages including Ingush, Tsez and Burmeso, situate Mian within its typological context, highlighting parallels with restricted and non-canonical agreement systems elsewhere. Our analysis casts doubt on functional explanations of agreement as reference tracking, since Mian shows no compensatory strategies when agreement is absent. The Mian case thus sharpens the theoretical understanding of restricted morphological systems and their acquisition, and it broadens the typology of agreement phenomena.

metadata.title: English verb placement in Norwegian/English bilinguals: A Micro-cue approach
metadata.description: The Micro-cue Model (Westergaard 2009) has been used to explain monolingual first and third language acquisition (Westergaard 2021) but has never been applied to simultaneous bilingual first language acquisition. We fill this gap by considering data on verb placement in English from four bilingual Norwegian/English girls, showing that they display four different patterns of cross-linguistic influence. We argue that the Micro-cue Model is perfect for capturing this variation, as it assumes that the different instantiations of verb placement and residual V2 in English are acquired separately.

metadata.title: An exoskeletal grammar approach to linguistic flexibility
metadata.description: This paper shows how a simple and robust version of an exoskeletal grammar model (dubbed the Exoskeletal Frame Model) is able to account for two ubiquitous types of linguistic flexibility, namely argument structure flexibility and lexical creativity. In both areas, it is concluded that an exoskeletal model should be preferred to a traditional lexicalist or endoskeletal model. The tenor of the paper is somewhat programmatic, seeking to make clear the principled differences between endoskeletalism on the one hand and exoskeletalism on the other, and simultaneously trying to point out the essential motivation for adopting the exoskeletal approach.

metadata.title: Introduction
metadata.description: This volume explores issues relating to language variation, acquisition, and change. It consists of 27 chapters that illuminate these issues from a range of different methodological, empirical, and theoretical perspectives. Many chapters also combine two or even three of the themes, illustrating that they are linked and that such combinations increase our understanding of a particular phenomenon.

metadata.title: A dictionary and grammatical sketch of Beja (Sudan)
metadata.description: This book contains a Beja-English-French dictionary, the first one to focus on the central and southern varieties of this Cushitic language as spoken in eastern Sudan, an appendix of clitics and affixes, an English-Beja reversal index, a French-Beja reversal index, and a grammatical sketch. The dictionary and its appendices contain over 8,000 entries and sub-entries. It is the largest dictionary on this language, and the sole one which is systematically organized by roots (the alphabetical order considers consonants and vowels), with all their variants and derived forms (also cross-referenced alphabetically). Lemmas contain the base form and all the derived forms of a root with all relevant information about parts of speech, verb categories, gender, source of loan words, etymologies, morphological, grammatical, sociolinguistic, encyclopaedic information, synonyms, antonyms, and examples. Literal translations of compound words and examples are provided when needed. Stress, tone, and phonetic forms are only mentioned when unpredictable from the rules mentioned in the grammatical sketch. The grammatical sketch contains sections on phonology, morphology (including compounds, evaluative morphology, and interjections), TAM (including verbal complex predicates), elements of syntax (including complex utterances), and information and discourse structures. This work is mainly intended as a resource for linguists, in particular specialist of Cushitic and Semitic languages, and can also serve as a resource for speakers and learners of Beja.

metadata.title: Variation in word meanings
metadata.description: Humans use language to convey meanings through spoken or signed expressions. However, the way languages divide the world into words varies. For example, the word laŋ in the language Belhare denotes the part of the body that reaches from the hip to the toes. In comparison, English speakers divide this area into two words: foot and leg . Languages thus combine meanings and express them with the same word; a phenomenon called colexification. In the approximately 6,500-7,000 languages of the world, meanings are combined in a wide variety of ways. This raises the following questions: How can we study language variation in word meanings? What patterns of variation occur and what causes them? I investigate these questions in this book. The aim of the book is twofold. First, language comparison is only possible if data are presented in a format that is accessible to humans and computers. Thus, I use a computer-assisted approach that provides a framework for managing large datasets and facilitates expert-driven reviews. This approach allows for both qualitative and quantitative analyses by integrating methods from computer science and linguistics. I illustrate the applicability of this approach by presenting a lexical database with data on words and concept properties for 39 languages. Second, language variation in word meanings is not random. While language is a product of history, culture, cognition, and coincidence, disentangling the different effects is a challenge. Yet, there are similarities in the way languages structure their vocabularies, which is evidence that there are constraints. By focusing on common cognitive dimensions that lead to the connections of certain meanings, the studies provide insights into overarching patterns.

metadata.title: Advancing interdisciplinarity in empirical translation research
metadata.description: This volume reflects the vast range of research sub-fields in contemporary translation and interpreting studies, including specialized translation, machine translation, and audio-visual translation. At the same time, the chapters illustrate the intrinsic interdisciplinary foundations of translation studies, highlighting its connection to specific linguistic subfields and applied branches. Among the linguistic fields, the strongest ties here are with contrastive linguistics and corpus linguistics, while its connection to practical applications is evident particularly in its focus on developing effective translator training methods.

metadata.title: Advancing interdisciplinarity in empirical translation research
metadata.description: Simultaneous interpreting (SI) is a cognitively difficult task which requires specialized training and continued learning to deliver the best performance. Even with full attention, occasional errors in interpreting are inevitable, and they are likely to rise in longer sessions. Nowadays, with the advances in deep learning, we are witnessing an increase in the quality of automatic simultaneous speech translation (ASST). However, compared to human interpretation, whose output is the spoken word, the ASST model creates a translated transcription of the original. The presented study assesses the state of the art by analysing translation departures in human SI (professional and trainee interpreters) and ASST systems. Two terminologically rich speeches, delivered by non-native English speakers, were remotely interpreted by two M.A. interpreting students, and one professional interpreter, to Czech. We had the speeches translated also by an in-house speech translation system. Our quality assessment focuses on content transfer from the original speech, extending Barik’s taxonomy (1971). Our findings reveal that trainee interpreters outperformed the professional one in multiple areas, such as avoiding over-reliance on original structure or excessive use of demonstrative pronouns. In comparison, the ASST model translated more literally, with outputs having fewer translation departures than human interpretations.

metadata.title: ``Default translation'': how free of fault? An exploratory comparison of NMT and human translation
metadata.description: The chapter centres around an exploratory extension of the concept of ‘default translation’ proposed by Halverson (2015, 2019), to study and compare the output of professional translators, trainees and NMT systems, for the purpose of cognitive modelling of translation as well as assessing NMT performance in terms of how successfully it imitates translation which is a product of human cognition. The data is drawn from translations of the same source text by 4 NMT systems (Google Translate, MS Bing, Systran, DeepL), 6 translation trainees and 6 professional translators. The data sets are compared quantitatively, based on a specific metric developed for the purpose of the study, as well as qualitatively, focusing on the solution-type distance between NMT and human translations. The source text was selected based on specific criteria to suit the default mode of translation and the human translations were obtained in a specific translation regime elicited by the instructions, designed to bring out ‘default translation’, here understood as a relatively routinized and uninterrupted mode (rather than phase) of translating. The main findings obtained are, firstly, convincing evidence of DeepL approximating human translations most successfully at collocational level and outperforming the other NMT systems, with a noticeable gap between DeepL and the other systems (and a minimal gap between DeepL and human translations), and, secondly, another solution pattern distinguishing human translations from DeepL, leading to the formulation of the Naturalness Impulse Hypothesis.

metadata.title: Advancing interdisciplinarity in empirical translation research
metadata.description: Since 2013, Dan Harmon and Justin Roiland’s postmodernist TV show Rick and Morty has staged a science-fictional world filled with dark and nonsensical humour and a tinge of nihilistic philosophy. The chapter offers an analysis of Rick & Morty’s invented terms that parody the genre, and their French translations in the dubbed version of the TV show. The authors use all the genre’s tools, including linguistic creativity, to ground their original world, and to generate humour. Using contrastive linguistic tools, such as semantic and morphosyntactic analysis, as well as translation studies theories and approaches, especially the notion of Nida’s dynamic equivalence, functionalist approaches to translation and previous research on translating humour, the chapter aims for a better understanding of the translation of parodic elements in a science-fictional context, especially in relation to the visual content. The chapter offers a model for evaluating the fluency of both generic and humorous terms in the target language, using linguistic criteria, while also taking into consideration all the constraints involved in translating audiovisual material, as well as the relationship between text and image. Translation strategies may create distinct effects on the target audience as fictive terms are necessarily connected to the visual and narrative content. The analysis aims to provide a refined vision of the priorities and restrictions in play during the translation process of novum parody. Thus the chapter highlights the close relationship between text, image and translation choices. Translators prioritize one of the aspects of the invented terms (humour, parody or genre) according to the audiovisual context. The chapter also offers to validate the proposed model by analysing another audiovisual work, Futurama, in order to confirm the hypotheses.

metadata.title: The drafting style of employment agreements and employment offer letters: A corpus-based approach
metadata.description: Plain English is language that can be understood by the layperson. Over the decades, scholars and linguists have advocated the drafting of plain English texts in the legal field (Tiersma 1999; Tiersma & Solan 2012; Williams 2023). Nonetheless, many legal documents are still drawn up in the most intricate form, which is referred to as legalese. Even contracts addressed to non-native speakers of English (such as employment agreements) tend to be drafted in an archaic style. In this respect, there seems to be a significant difference between employment agreements and employment offer letters. This chapter is aimed at bringing to the surface the nuances between these two types of contracts. In particular, it unveils whether legalese features are used in both types of documents and if their drafting style is formal or informal. To this purpose, two corpora are constructed and analyzed: one composed of employment agreements, and the other of employment offer letters. This analysis highlights recurrent phrases, formulaic expressions, and legal terminology in such documents. The chapter findings highlight that there seems to be a more pervasive use of plain English language in employment offer letters, whereas employment contracts tend to be drafted in legalese. The chapter presents implications of corpus-based analyses in translation studies. More precisely, it shows how corpus-driven activities can be adopted in the translation process. Its rigorous methods and principles may, in fact, be replicated in other fields, thus fostering interdisciplinarity in translation research.

metadata.title: Using diachronic corpora to translate emerging or new specialized fields
metadata.description: This chapter discusses the use of short diachronic corpora to provide translators with conceptual and terminological information considered useful when translating documents dealing with emerging or new medical specialties. While the link between specialized translation and corpora is now well established, the use of diachronic corpora, and in particular short diachronic corpora (i.e. covering only a few years) for translation purposes remains largely uncharted territory. The work presented in this chapter is based on the assumption that the use of diachronic information will provide translators with the cognitive and terminological information needed to understand the conceptual organization of complex specialized fields, particularly when it comes to reporting scientific advances or innovations through translation. The chapter is based on the study of a specialized corpus, covering a short period of time (24 years, from 1993 to 2017), in the field of nanomedicine applied to cancer treatment. This corpus-based study serves as a starting point for assessing which types of diachronic information are most useful and which are not, from a translation point of view. The final part of the chapter will be devoted to a discussion of the advantages and limitations of such an approach and how it can be implemented in the context of translator training.

metadata.title: Schodiště z mramoru and the marble staircase: English divergent counterparts of Czech postmodifying prepositional phrases
metadata.description: The chapter explores the English translation correspondences of Czech postmodifying prepositional phrases, focussing on the rare cases of formal divergence. The contrastive analysis relies on material drawn from the parallel corpus InterCorp. The results reveal the impact of the register (fiction vs. non-fiction) and direction of translation on the degree of congruence between the counterparts. Drawing on both Czech texts translated into English (CS(en)) and English-to-Czech translations (cs(EN)), the study catalogues the recurrent patterns of correspondence and describes their formal and semantic properties. The choice of a particular divergent counterpart was found to be related mostly to the typological differences between Czech and English, as manifested, for instance, in the correspondence between Czech postmodifying prepositional phrases and English premodifying nouns or postmodification by participial clauses with semantically weak predicates.

metadata.title: A corpus-driven investigation of translation strategies for prenominal complex adjectives
metadata.description: This chapter investigates a parallel corpus comprising original German texts and Italian translations from the field of tourism, with the objective of examining different translation strategies applied to Prenominal Complex Adjectives (PCAs). The study first categorizes German PCAs into seven groups. A regression analysis is then conducted to assess translation strategy frequencies. The results display a strong statistical correlation between categories and translation strategies, with a marked tendency to preserve the original syntactic structures. A qualitative analysis is carried out on the more unusual and transformational translation strategy of transposition in order to test its effectiveness for a complex syntactic structure characterized by two-directional syntactic reference. Results show that certain aspects of cognitive complexity in the original PCAs may encourage or trigger the application of transposition as a translation strategy for PCAs.

metadata.title: Navigating translation effort through translation process research database to unravel dimensions of script and text direction
metadata.description: This chapter delves into the multifaceted interplay between different script and text direction in translation, exploring the nuanced technical, temporal, and cognitive effort exerted by translators. We utilize a methodological approach that combines eye-tracking and keylogging data with 2-way ANOVA, using a series of empirical features (such as insertion, deletion, pause-to-word ratio, total number of fixations, etc.) to measure indicators of effort in translation. The study reveals elevated effort when translating between languages with different scripts and text directions. The findings underscore that script differences may introduce challenges at orthographic, lexical, and segment levels, while text direction differences augment spatial orientation demands. Notably, while both factors individually increased translation effort, an interaction effect between script difference and text direction difference was not observed, suggesting distinct cognitive processes for each challenge. These revelations hold profound implications for translation pedagogy, advocating for tailored training approaches and the integration of specific translation strategies to navigate these difficulties. The chapter contributes empirical insights to translation research, emphasizing the pivotal role of scriptural and spatial attributes in the translation process.

metadata.title: Data visualization in corpus-based contrastive linguistics and translation and interpreting studies
metadata.description: While inferential statistics are indispensable in comparative corpus studies such as those conducted in contrastive linguistics (CL) and translation and interpreting studies (TIS), it is equally important for researchers to develop an intuitive understanding of the data. Visualizations serve as a key tool for this purpose. In this contribution we distinguish three types of comparative corpus data commonly encountered by contrastive linguists and translation scholars: language-specific data, undirected comparative data, and directed comparative data. We discuss three main visualization techniques: proportional visualizations, graph-based visualizations and ordination techniques. We explore the strengths and limitations of these approaches, point out some caveats and provide scripts (in R and Python) to enable readers to replicate the analyses.

metadata.title: Linguistik für Lehramtsstudierende
metadata.description: Linguistik für Lehramtsstudierende bietet eine grammatische Beschreibung der deutschen Standardsprache und zahlreicher Variationsphänomene. Die Darstellung setzt bei sprachlichen Formen an und untersucht deren Funktionen. Die Betrachtung bewegt sich von der größeren Ebene des Satzes über kleinere sprachliche Bausteine (Wortgruppen, Wörter, Wortbausteine, Silben) bis hin zu den kleinsten lautlichen Ebenen (Lautklassen und einzelne Laute). Den Abschluss bildet ein Kapitel zur Schreibung (Graphematik) des Deutschen. Auf allen sprachlichen Ebenen stellen wir zahlreiche Bezüge zu Schule und Vermittlung her. Begrifflich orientieren wir uns an dem aktuellen, von der Kultusministerkonferenz zustimmend zur Kenntnis genommenen Verzeichnis grundlegender grammatischer Fachausdrücke . In erster Linie ist dieses Lehrbuch als vertiefendes Begleitmaterial zu ein- und weiterführenden linguistischen Lehrveranstaltungen konzipiert. Es vermittelt vor allem Techniken der linguistischen Analyse und Reflexion. Viele Übungsaufgaben samt ausführlich kommentierter Lösungen ermöglichen auch den Einsatz im Selbststudium und zur berufsbegleitenden Weiterbildung.

metadata.title: The material culture of the Teop people of Bougainville
metadata.description: In this text collection, nine Teop authors and one Teop graphic artist document the use of palms, trees, bamboo and other plants in their material culture. The book consists of six main parts. Following the introductory chapters on the Teop language and the historical context of the text collection in Part I, Parts II to V contain 32 Teop texts with illustrations and English translations on the topics of plants, house-building, canoe-building and traditional fishing techniques. Part VI provides all the Teop texts and their translations, with an additional linguistic analysis and glossing of each word in interlinearized format. The chapters in Part I and the brief introductions to the texts in Parts II to V are by the editor, who also produced the English translations in collaboration with the Teop authors, as well as the linguistic analysis and glossing in Part VI.

metadata.title: Lexical functions: The naked truth
metadata.description: This book introduces lexical functions, a formal tool which ensures a systematic homo- geneous description of two complementary families of relations between lexical units: • derivations – paradigmatic lexical functions; • collocations, which are constrained lexical combinations – syntagmatic lexical functions. Each lexical function is associated with a specific meaning and once it is applied to a given lexical unit, which is seen as its argument, the function returns, as its value, the set of (near-)synonymous lexical entities which express this meaning depending on the argument. As an example, the paradigmatic lexical function S1 is associated with the meaning ‘someone/something which does/is...’, and the syntagmatic lexical function Magn is associated with the meaning ‘very’/‘intense(ly)’ as illustrated below. S₁ ( felony ) = felon S₁ ( gossip (V) ) = gossiper ; busybody S₁ ( disappointing ) = disappointment ; bummer Magn( penalty ) = harsh , heavy , hefty , severe , stiff Magn( fight (V) ) = fiercely , ⌜ to the bitter end ⌝, ⌜ tooth and nail ⌝ Magn( bored ) = stiff [~], ⌜t o death ⌝, ⌜ to tears ⌝ The volume describes and illustrates (for English, French and Russian) the system of 66 simple standard lexical functions, which can be combined to form complex and config- urational lexical functions. Standard lexical functions are language-universal: they seem sufficient for the description of standard derivations and collocations of any language. (For unique and deviating derivations and collocations non-standard lexical functions are assumed.) Balancing conceptual depth with pedagogical effort, Lexical functions: The naked truth guides readers from foundational notions to the full system of lexical func- tions, concluding with their role in modeling the network structure of natural language lexicons.

metadata.title: Donkeys, bishops, and the distinction between weak and strong definites
metadata.description: Much recent work on definiteness has assumed that definite descriptions come in two types, weak and strong. Weak definites make use of a simple situation-relative uniqueness operator; strong definites add to this a variable available to dynamic binding. Drawing on evidence from Mandarin, Jenks (2018) influentially proposed that strong definites but not weak definites can serve as donkey anaphors. We show that this claim is incorrect for Mandarin as well as for German and English. Certain special cases of donkey anaphora nevertheless have diagnostic value for the distinction between weak and strong definites. We discuss two. First, in structures where there is no dynamic quantifier available to serve as an antecedent, strong definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. Second, in so-called bishop sentences, the uniqueness requirement of the weak definite is not met; in these cases weak definite descriptions cannot serve as donkey anaphors. We apply these tests to definites in German, English, and Mandarin. Our results indicate that English the and Mandarin bare nouns are always weak definites, but also that important aspects of crosslinguistic variation with respect to weak definites remain to be explained.

metadata.title: Vague predicates, crisp judgments
metadata.description: Nez Perce is a language with a dedicated comparative morpheme and crisp judgments in its comparatives, but with no means to express differential measurement in its comparative. These data can be captured by two different types of analyses: either Nez Perce has a negative setting of the Degree Semantics Parameter ([±DSP]) (Beck et al., 2009), along with a comparative operator that allows manipulation of context (Klein, 1980), or it has a positive setting of said parameter, but the comparative operator does not provide a slot for a differential degree argument. We show that the “degreeless” analysis of gradable adjectives in Nez Perce provides a unified and simple explanation for a cluster of additional properties of the language. At the same time, our findings draw attention to hitherto unattested variation within degreeless languages: other [-DSP] languages like Motu (Beck et al., 2009), Washo (Bochnak, 2015) and Warlpiri (Bowler, 2016) lack the Klein-style comparative operator present in Nez Perce.

metadata.title: Third readings by semantic scope lowering: Prolepsis in Tiwa
metadata.description: Tiwa (Tibeto-Burman; India) attitude reports allow for proleptic objects, base-generated in the matrix clause but semantically related to a bound pronoun in the embedded clause. Unlike prolepsis in German (Salzmann, 2017b) and Nez Perce (Deal, 2018), which only allow for classic de re readings of the proleptic object, Tiwa prolepsis supports both classic de re and third readings. We provide an analysis that derives third readings via semantic scope lowering, an analytical relative of semantic reconstruction, and consider cross-linguistic implications.
